title: Misleading Charts & Visualization Pitfalls
interviewAnswer: A visualization can be numerically correct and still mislead through truncated axes, inappropriate aggregation, dual axes, area encodings or selective time windows.
keyPoints: Preserve meaningful baselines when magnitude comparisons matter.
why: Misleading Charts & Visualization Pitfalls appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.
intuition: Preserve meaningful baselines when magnitude comparisons matter.
deepDive: A visualization can be numerically correct and still mislead through truncated axes, inappropriate aggregation, dual axes, area encodings or selective time windows. Show uncertainty where relevant. Avoid aggregation that hides heterogeneity. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.
workedExample: A conversion chart starting the y-axis at 49% makes a 49% to 50% increase look enormous.
commonMistakes: Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.
followUps: What assumptions does Misleading Charts & Visualization Pitfalls make?
How would you validate or debug Misleading Charts & Visualization Pitfalls in practice?
production: In production, validate assumptions on real data, monitor the quantities that can drift, and keep a simple baseline so added complexity has a measurable reason to exist.
